text: Arch Linux is an open source, rolling release Linux distribution that is kept up-to-date by regularly updating its individual software components. It provides monthly "snapshots" used as installation media and is intentionally minimal, requiring users to configure the system manually during installation to include only the software they need. The distribution uses Pacman, a package manager specifically developed for Arch Linux, to install, remove, and update software packages, with support for automatic dependency resolution. Pacman manages binary packages with a .pkg.tar.zst extension (zstd compression) or .pkg.tar.xz, and packages are compiled for the x86-64 architecture. All official packages are obtained from the Arch Linux package tree. The Arch User Repository (AUR) is a community-driven repository that hosts PKGBUILD scripts for software not included in the official repositories or alternative versions of existing packages; these scripts are built using the Arch build system (ABS) via the makepkg command and are not binary packages. AUR packages can be built manually or installed using AUR helper tools, though Arch developers emphasize that automatic downloading and execution of PKGBUILDs is not included in official repositories due to security risks, such as a malware incident on 19 July 2025 involving a modified Firefox build that was a remote access trojan (RAT). The AUR allows users to contribute PKGBUILDs, with those receiving 10 or more votes or over 1% usage from pkgstats eligible for promotion to the extra repository. The official repositories include core, extra, community, and testing, with community merged into extra in May 2023 and the unstable repository discontinued in July 2008; core-staging and extra-staging are used for rebuilds but are discouraged for use. The distribution does not schedule releases or provide traditional versions, instead relying on a rolling release model where packages are frequently updated, allowing systems to stay current. Manual interventions are occasionally required, as noted in the news section. Arch Linux's design emphasizes simplicity and transparency, avoiding complex abstractions and instead promoting direct user interaction through clean, well-documented configuration files, which has earned it a reputation as a distribution for advanced users who prefer the command line. The current logo was designed by Thayer Williams in 2007. Installation can be done manually via the Arch Wiki or automatically using the default 'archinstall' script introduced in April 2021, or through the 'pacstrap' utility. The distribution supports x86-64 processors and originally only targeted IA-32 CPUs, with the first x86-64 ISO released in April 2006. i686 support ended with the February 2017 ISO, making it unsupported in November 2017, and the community derivative Arch Linux 32 continues support for 32-bit hardware. The migration to systemd as the default init system began in August 2012 and became standard in October 2012, replacing the earlier SysV-style init. Until Pacman version 4.0.0, package signing was not supported, and packages were not verified for authenticity; however, package signing became mandatory for new builds in November 2011 and fully enabled by default in March 2012. The Arch build system enables source compilation and allows users to create custom PKGBUILD scripts to build packages compatible with Pacman. Arch Linux includes both libre and nonfree software, with the default kernel containing proprietary blobs, meaning it is not endorsed by the GNU project; the linux-libre kernel can be installed via the AUR or Parabola's repositories. The distribution is working toward making all official packages reproducible, allowing verification of package integrity across different environments. Arch Linux has a comprehensive community-run documentation site, the ArchWiki. The project was initiated in March 2002 by Judd Vinet, who chose the name for its meaning of "the principal," as in "arch-enemy," and stepped down in October 2007, transferring leadership to Aaron Griffin. Griffin stepped down in February 2020 after a voting period, transferring control to Levente Polyak, with a new two-year term added for the Project Leader position. In March 2021, developers considered porting packages to x86_64-v3 (Intel Haswell-era processors), and in February 2022, debug packages were introduced. In late 2021, Pacman 6.0 was released with support for parallel downloads. On 14 August 2025, the Arch User Repository, forums, and website were hit by a distributed denial-of-service attack, causing temporary unavailability and severely slowing or blocking AUR downloads. SteamOS 3.0, used in the Steam Deck, is based on Arch Linux. CachyOS is a gaming-focused distribution based on Arch Linux. Projects like PacBSD and Arch Hurd are adapting Arch Linux tools to other kernels, and the Arch Linux ARM project aims to port the distribution to ARM devices like the Raspberry Pi. Arch Linux has received reviews from OSNews, LWN.net, Tux Machines, and DistroWatch Weekly, with Greg Kroah-Hartman praising its performance and community feedback. In a 2023 DistroWatch poll, 17% of respondents used Arch and 30% used an Arch derivative, and as of 2025, Arch holds the third-highest average rating (9.18) on DistroWatch, behind only Artix Linux and BigLinux, both Arch derivatives.
